## Session 13 — Presentation day {background-color="#7A003C"}

Team presentations of the major project.

**All group reports due at start of class.**

::: {.notes}
Collect reports at the door. Confirm A2L submissions. Announce
presentation order (should have been emailed by Monday). Keep pace -
7 teams × 20 min = 140 min, plus break, plus wrap. Tight.
:::

## Today's schedule

| Time | Activity                                    |
|------|---------------------------------------------|
| 0:00 | Instructor welcome + peer-eval brief (5 min) |
| 0:05 | Presentations begin (~20 min per team)      |
| 1:30 | Break (15 min)                              |
| 1:45 | Presentations continue                       |
| 2:55 | Instructor wrap-up + course reflection (5 min) |

::: {.notes}
Adjust for team count. If 5 teams, generous timing. If 7-8 teams,
tight. Have a timekeeper (you or a volunteer). Ring a bell at 15 min
warning, 18 min stop.
:::

## Peer evaluation

Each student evaluates the other teams (not their own):

- **Clarity of research question** (1-5)
- **Methodology soundness** (1-5)
- **Quality of findings** (1-5)
- **Recommendation strength** (1-5)
- **Presentation delivery** (1-5)
- One-sentence: **most compelling insight**
- One-sentence: **most useful improvement**

Submitted anonymously via A2L by end of day.

::: {.notes}
Peer eval doesn't directly affect grades - it's formative feedback
for the presenting teams and for calibrating instructor grading.
Some instructors weight peer eval into project grade; this course
doesn't for simplicity.
:::

## What I'm looking for as instructor

- **Business problem clearly stated** — one sentence
- **Design matched to the question** — no over- or under-engineering
- **Analysis appropriate** — right tests, right visuals
- **Findings interpreted managerially** — what would you do?
- **Limitations honest** — no over-claiming
- **All members contributing** — visible team engagement

::: {.notes}
Read this out at the start. Sets expectations. Students perform to
the rubric you announce.
:::

## Time management

- **Hard stop at 20 minutes** — no exceptions
- Practise your timing beforehand
- If you finish early, that's fine — better than running long
- Q&A: 5-7 min after each presentation

::: {.notes}
Running long is the most common failure. Cut off politely: "Thanks
team, let's take one Q&A question and move on." Fairness matters -
every team gets the same slot.
:::

## Questions to expect

Instructor + peer questions typically probe:

- **"Why this design and not X?"**
- **"How confident are you in finding Y?"**
- **"What would you do differently with more time/budget?"**
- **"What's the most surprising thing you learned?"**
- **"How would the recommendation change if [assumption] were wrong?"**

::: {.notes}
Prep the class - these are the standard MR questions. Students who
anticipate them present more confidently.
:::

## Presenting well

- **Face the audience** (not the screen)
- **Slow down** — nerves speed you up
- **One point per slide**
- **Charts, not tables** where possible
- **Rehearse the transitions** between speakers

Every team member speaks. Roughly equal time.

::: {.notes}
Standard presentation coaching. Some students will be strong; others
will need coaching. Give private feedback after class where helpful.
:::

## Break (15 min) after first block {background-color="#FDBF57"}

Come back promptly.

::: {.notes}
Circulate during the break. Give quick informal feedback to teams
that have presented. Reset the room for the next block.
:::

# Wrap-up and course reflection {background-color="#7A003C"}

## Thirteen weeks recap

You've built the full arc:

1. Defined a research problem (Wk 1)
2. Chose a design (Wk 2)
3. Sampled + measured (Wks 3-4)
4. Handled qualitative + quantitative data (Wks 5-9)
5. Reasoned about causation (Wk 10)
6. Modelled drivers (Wk 11)
7. Reported and presented (Wks 12-13)

::: {.notes}
Reinforce the arc. Students often lose sight of the whole in the
week-to-week grind. The final Wednesday is when you help them see
what they've built.
:::

## What you can now do

- Read a research brief and design an appropriate study
- Write a defensible sampling plan
- Design a questionnaire that survives peer review
- Analyse survey data in R with appropriate tests
- Interpret regression and factor-analytic output
- Write and deliver a decision-oriented report
- Discuss research ethics with sophistication

::: {.notes}
Encouragement moment. Frame these as employable skills. Point
students to MRIA membership, R user groups, and portfolio-building
opportunities.
:::

## Grading and feedback

- Reports: graded within 2 weeks; comments returned via A2L
- Final grades: submitted per program deadline
- Individual questions on grading: office hours or email

::: {.notes}
Be specific about when grades will be back. Students obsess about
this - clarity reduces email volume.
:::

## Continuing on

For students continuing in MR or insights:

- **Read journals:** JMR, Marketing Science, JCR, IJRM
- **Join a body:** MRIA-ARIM (Canada), ESOMAR, Insights Association
- **Keep coding:** R for MR is a rare and valuable skill
- **Study one advanced method deeply:** conjoint, MaxDiff, hierarchical Bayes, causal ML

::: {.notes}
Point students at real next steps. Some will pursue this seriously;
others just wanted the MBA credit. Both are fine.
:::
